about.title: About Bible Parlor
about.meta: By The Bible Parlor Team · July 21, 2026
about.intro: Bible Parlor exists because serious Bible study tools should not sit behind a paywall or a subscription tier. We built a King James Version study platform that runs in a browser, loads on a phone as easily as a desktop, and gives readers the same depth of reference material that used to require a shelf of print concordances, atlases, and lexicons.
about.mission.title: Our mission
about.mission.body: Our mission is simple: make rigorous Bible study tools free and mobile-friendly for anyone who wants to read the text closely — pastors preparing a sermon on a Tuesday night, a small-group leader building discussion questions, a student tracing a Greek word through the New Testament, or a reader who just wants to know what a place name in Acts actually looked like on a map. None of that should require paying a monthly fee or being tied to a desktop program. Bible Parlor runs on bibleparlor.com, works on any modern browser, and keeps every core feature free.
about.offers.title: What Bible Parlor offers
about.tool.reader.title: Study Bible Reader
about.tool.reader.desc: The full King James Version with chapter and verse navigation, tap-to-view cross-references, and inline access to Strong’s numbers on every word. This is the home base that links out to every other tool.
about.tool.strongs.title: Strong’s Concordance
about.tool.strongs.desc: The complete Strong’s numbering system — Hebrew H1 through H8674 and Greek G1 through G5624 — mapped to every occurrence of each word across the KJV text, so you can see a word’s original-language root and every other verse where it appears.
about.tool.atlas.title: Biblical Atlas
about.tool.atlas.desc: An interactive map of places named in Scripture, with markers tied to the verses that mention them. Trace Paul’s journeys, locate the cities of the exodus route, or find where a prophecy names a specific town, all on the same map layer.
about.tool.lexicon.title: Word Study Lexicon
about.tool.lexicon.desc: A full lexicon view for any Strong’s-numbered Hebrew or Greek word, showing its range of meaning, grammatical form, and every verse in the KJV where the underlying word occurs — the same information a Hebrew or Greek dictionary would give you, without needing to own one.
about.tool.explorer.title: Explorer
about.tool.explorer.desc: Full-text and topical search across the KJV, letting you search by phrase, word, or topic and get every matching verse back instantly, with links into Strong’s and the Atlas for anything that comes up.
about.tool.builder.title: Sermon Builder
about.tool.builder.desc: A workspace for assembling an outline with supporting verses, cross-references, and notes pulled directly from your study — built for pastors and teachers who need to go from research to a usable outline without switching apps.
about.tool.connect.title: Bible Connect
about.tool.connect.desc: A private space for a church, ministry, or study group to gather online. Group creators can post announcements to a main board, open topical chats, and let members share sermons, notes, and scripture references with each other between services.
about.tool.teams.title: Teams
about.tool.teams.desc: A church-scoped workspace for tracking Bible studies with prospective and returning students. Teachers schedule sessions, log follow-up outcomes, and hand off students between each other, while a church admin manages membership, teaching teams, and baptism records for the congregation.
about.kjv.title: Why the King James Version
about.kjv.body: We built Bible Parlor on the King James Version for two practical reasons. First, the KJV is in the public domain, which means we can host, link, and cross-reference the full text without licensing restrictions that limit what a study tool can do with the underlying data. Second, the KJV has nearly two centuries of established cross-reference and concordance work built around it — most notably James Strong’s exhaustive concordance from 1890 — so the Hebrew and Greek word mapping that powers our Strong’s tool and Word Study lexicon is mature, well-tested, and consistent across the entire text. That existing scholarly infrastructure is what lets us offer deep word-level study for free rather than building a new reference system from scratch.
about.values.title: Our values
about.value.paywalls.label: No paywalls
about.value.paywalls.body: Every tool — the Reader, Strong’s, Atlas, Word Study, Explorer, Sermon Builder, Bible Connect, and Teams — is free to use in full. We do not gate features behind a subscription.
about.value.ads.label: No ads
about.value.ads.body: We do not run banner ads, video ads, or sponsored content inside the study experience. The page you study on is the page you get.
about.value.data.label: No data selling
about.value.data.body: We do not sell user data to advertisers or third parties. Your reading history, notes, and sermon drafts are yours.
about.value.mobile.label: Built for mobile
about.value.mobile.body: Every tool is designed to work as well on a phone in a pew or a kitchen table as it does on a desktop in a study.
about.contact.title: Contact
about.contact.body: Questions, corrections, or feature requests are welcome. Reach the team at contact@bibleparlor.com.

blog.strongs.p1: Strong’s Concordance is a reference system that assigns a unique number to every distinct Hebrew, Aramaic, or Greek word underlying the King James Version of the Bible. Instead of guessing at the original-language word behind an English translation, you look up the number attached to any English word in the text and go directly to the Hebrew or Greek term it translates. It remains the most widely used tool for original-language Bible study more than 130 years after its publication.
blog.strongs.h2.who: Who was James Strong, and why 1890?
blog.strongs.p.james1: James Strong (1822–1894) was a professor of biblical literature at Drew Theological Seminary in Madison, New Jersey. He spent over three decades compiling what he titled The Exhaustive Concordance of the Bible, published in 1890. The word “exhaustive” was literal: Strong and his team of assistants indexed every single occurrence of every word in the King James Version — not just significant theological terms, but every word, including common ones like “and” and “the.”
blog.strongs.p.james2: Strong’s core innovation was separating two jobs that earlier concordances mixed together. A concordance’s first job is to list every verse where an English word occurs. Its second, much harder job is to identify which original-language word stands behind that English word in each case — because translators often render the same Hebrew or Greek word with different English words, and sometimes render different original words with the same English word. Strong solved the second problem by assigning a permanent reference number to every original-language word and printing that number next to each entry, so a reader with no Hebrew or Greek training could still trace the original word directly.
blog.strongs.p.numbering: Strong’s system uses two separate number ranges, one for each testament’s source language family:
blog.strongs.p.howH: Every word in the Old Testament carries an “H” number; every word in the New Testament carries a “G” number. The numbers themselves don’t follow alphabetical or thematic order — they were assigned roughly in the sequence Strong’s team encountered and catalogued the words, so H1 is not necessarily more “important” than H8674. What matters is that each number always points to exactly the same original-language word, no matter where it appears in Scripture. Because the number is fixed, you can jump from any English word in any verse straight to its Hebrew or Greek root without needing to read Hebrew or Greek yourself.
blog.strongs.p.entry: Each Strong’s entry typically includes the transliterated original word, its root or derivation, a grammatical classification (noun, verb, adjective, and so on), a definition or range of meaning, and — critically — a list of the different English words the KJV translators used to render it throughout the Bible. That last part matters more than people expect: it shows you at a glance whether a word is translated consistently or scattered across several different English renderings depending on context.
blog.strongs.p.wt.intro: The clearest way to see Strong’s system in action is to work through a real verse.
blog.strongs.p.wt.logos: The English word “Word,” capitalized here as a title for Christ, carries the Greek Strong’s number G3056, the noun logos. In koine Greek, logos means far more than a single spoken or written word — it carries the sense of a reasoned account, a message, or an underlying rational principle that governs and explains something. Greek philosophy, particularly Stoic thought, had already used logos to describe the rational principle ordering the universe. John’s Gospel takes that loaded philosophical term and applies it to Christ: the eternal, reasoning Word who was “with God” and “was God” from the beginning, and who — as John 1:14 states — “was made flesh, and dwelt among us.”
blog.strongs.p.wt.occurrences: Looking up G3056 in a Strong’s tool shows you that logos appears roughly 330 times in the New Testament, translated most often as “word” but also as “saying,” “account,” “reason,” “communication,” and other terms depending on context. Reading through even a handful of those other occurrences — for example, Luke 4:32 (“his word was with power”) or Hebrews 4:12 (“the word of God is quick, and powerful”) — builds a fuller sense of the term than the single word “Word” in John 1:1 can carry on its own.
blog.strongs.p.wt.value: This is the entire value of Strong’s Concordance in one example: an English reader with zero Greek training can see that “Word” in John 1:1 is not a generic term for speech, but a specific, philosophically loaded Greek noun that John deliberately chose to identify Christ with the eternal reasoning principle behind all creation.

blog.paul.p1: The book of Acts records three separate missionary journeys undertaken by Paul, covering roughly AD 46 to 57 and thousands of miles by land and sea across Asia Minor, Greece, and the eastern Mediterranean. Each journey has a distinct route, cast of companions, and turning point in Acts. Below is a city-by-city breakdown of all three, with the Acts passages that record each leg.
blog.paul.p.first.summary: This first journey established the pattern Paul would repeat: preach first in the synagogue, gather a mixed Jewish-and-Gentile following, face organized opposition, and appoint local elders before moving on. It also set up the theological controversy — whether Gentile converts needed to be circumcised and keep the Mosaic law — that the Jerusalem Council resolves in Acts 15.
blog.paul.p.second.summary: The second journey is the hinge point where the Christian mission moves decisively from Asia Minor into Greece. Philippi, Thessalonica, and Corinth all become recipient churches of New Testament letters — Philippians, 1 and 2 Thessalonians, and 1 and 2 Corinthians — making this route essential background for reading Paul’s epistles in context.
blog.paul.p.third.summary: The third journey produces some of Paul’s most theologically dense writing — most scholars place the writing of Romans during the three-month stay in Greece near the end of this journey, and 1 Corinthians during the extended Ephesus stay. It also ends the pattern of “journeys” altogether: after his arrest in Jerusalem, Paul’s remaining travel in Acts happens as a prisoner, culminating in the voyage to Rome recorded in Acts 27–28.

blog.inductive.crumb: How to Study the Bible Inductively
blog.inductive.h1: How to Study the Bible Inductively
blog.inductive.p1: Inductive Bible study is a method that starts with the text itself rather than with a conclusion you already hold. Instead of opening a passage looking to confirm a point you want to make, you work through three sequential steps — Observation, Interpretation, and Application — letting each step build on the last. The method comes from inductive reasoning generally: you gather specific details first, then draw a general conclusion from them, rather than starting with a general conclusion and hunting for verses to support it.
blog.inductive.p.threestep: The three steps are sequential and should not be skipped or reordered, because each one depends on the work done in the step before it.
blog.inductive.h3.step1: Step 1: Observation — what does the text actually say?
blog.inductive.p.step1: Observation means reading the passage slowly and noting exactly what is there before drawing any conclusions about what it means. This includes the literal wording, repeated words or phrases, connecting words like “therefore” or “but,” the grammatical subject and verb of each sentence, and the passage’s place in its surrounding paragraph or chapter. The goal at this stage is description, not interpretation — you are building an inventory of facts about the text.
blog.inductive.h3.step2: Step 2: Interpretation — what did it mean to its original audience?
blog.inductive.p.step2: Interpretation asks what the passage meant to the people who first received it, using the observations you gathered in step one plus relevant historical, cultural, and literary context. This is where you ask who wrote the passage, to whom, why, and under what circumstances — and where tools like a Bible atlas or a concordance for original-language words become essential, because meaning is anchored in a specific historical setting, not in whatever a modern reader assumes the words mean today.
blog.inductive.h3.step3: Step 3: Application — what does it mean for me now?
blog.inductive.p.step3: Application is the step where you ask how the meaning you established in step two should shape belief or action today. Application is only trustworthy when it is built on steps one and two — skipping straight to application without doing the observation and interpretation work first is exactly how a passage gets bent to say something it was never saying in context.
